newsitem.title: FRANCE: French analysts' comments on budget pact delay.
newsitem.headline: French analysts' comments on budget pact delay.

text.p: Following are comments from French analysts about reports from a meeting of European finance ministers in Luxembourg that France was seeking a period of reflection before a final agreement on the European Union's "stability pact".
SONJA GIBBS, BOND ANALYST, NOMURA INTERNATIONAL
The market has taken this very badly for obvious reasons, everybody was pinning their hopes on the Amsterdam summit but in reality the IGC doesn't finish until the end of June.

The risk is more that the market sees a real conflict between France and Germany - some of the comments coming out from (German finance minister Theo) Waigel sound unfriendly - even though in the longer run it does not mean an end to EMU if there's no stability pact in Amsterdam.

The combined votes of the centre-right and the bulk of the left ought to be able to get the National Assembly to sign off on this. It looks like they are trying to get them to tack on an employment clause.
The problem is, it also needs to be sold to the German public. Nobody was expecting an agreement today, it's not the time or the place, it was more a forum for discussion,
IAIN LINDSAY, SENIOR BOND ANALYST, CREDIT LYONNAIS
All that they've said is they want to think about it -- they're keeping their powder dry.

It would appear from this that the Socialist government is maybe a little more serious ultimately than some had taken them to be. (French Prime Minister Lionel) Jospin wants to maintain his credibility.

The nub of the problem - it's never really been the stability pact - is that the European central bank is seen as having an imbalance in its priorities...as long as that remains it's going to be an irritation. The French are just chipping away at the block as it were.
It's confirmaiton of the suspicions we all had - but we didn't know where in the diplomacy of all this they would want to strike.
It's a negative...(but) it's going to take more than this to make it all fall apart.
The process that we expected, that (the new Socialist government's) election promises would clash with the problems they have as a government, is materialising.
Whatever they (the French) proposed to the Germans, nothing seems to have come of it. Both sides have their interests and neither side can afford to appear weak.
Until they kiss and make up, we could see the franc go up and down.
